paper_description: This paper presents a unified schedulability test for global Earliest Deadline First (GEDF) and non-preemptive global Earliest Deadline First (NP-GEDF) multiprocessor scheduling. The test determines if a set of sporadic tasks with arbitrary relative deadlines and specified tardiness bounds can be scheduled such that these bounds are met. The tests are of pseudopolynomial time complexity and are applicable to hard, soft, and mixed real-time contexts.

formal_description.statement: t d -t 0 ≥ max(min(D i ), min(D k , p k -Θ k ))

variables.t_0: earliest instant such that for all t in [t_0, t_e), |τ_p(t)| >= m or fewer than |τ_p(t)| tasks from τ_p(t) execute at time t.
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k

assumptions: Job T_{k,j} misses its deadline by more than Θ_k.
t_e is the time when job T_{k,j} first becomes ready.
τ_p(t) is the set of tasks T_a such that for some b, T_{a,b} is pending at time t and T_{a,b} has higher priority than T_{k,j}.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a lower bound on the time interval between the earliest busy instant t_0 and the deadline t_d of a critical job T_{k,j} that is about to miss its tardiness bound.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma establishes a minimum duration for the interval where the system is busy with higher-priority tasks or non-preemptively executing lower-priority tasks before the critical job T_{k,j} can even start execution, given that T_{k,j} is destined to miss its deadline significantly.
steps: The release time of job T_{k,j} is r_{k,j} = t_d - D_k.
The predecessor job T_{k,j-1} finishes at time t' <= t_d - p_k + Θ_k.
By definition, t_e (when T_{k,j} becomes ready) is the later of its arrival time and its predecessor's completion time: t_e = max(r_{k,j}, t').
Therefore, t_e <= max(t_d - D_k, t_d - p_k + Θ_k).
Since t_0 <= t_e, we have t_0 <= max(t_d - D_k, t_d - p_k + Θ_k).
Rearranging this inequality to bound t_d - t_0 gives: t_d - t_0 >= min(t_d - (t_d - D_k), t_d - (t_d - p_k + Θ_k)) = min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k).
The proof also considers the case where t_0 > t_d - min(D_i), which implies t_0 > t_d - D_k, and uses properties of busy intervals to show that t_d - t_0 must be at least min(D_i).
Combining these, we get t_d - t_0 >= max(min(D_i), min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k)).
key_insights: The bound on t_d - t_0 is influenced by the relative deadline of the critical task (D_k) and its period minus its tardiness bound (p_k - Θ_k).
The minimum deadline of any task (min(D_i)) also plays a role in bounding the busy interval.

formal_description.statement: Each of I_CH(T_i), I_CL(T_i), and I_NC(T_i) is at most δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1, if i = k, and at most max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k), if i != k.

variables.I_CH(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_CH within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.I_CL(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_CL within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.I_NC(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_NC within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.δ_k: t_d - t_0 (duration of the busy interval).
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.
variables.t_e: time when job T_{k,j} first becomes ready.
variables.Γ: set of intervals within [t_e, t_d + Θ_k) where job T_{k,j} does not execute.

assumptions: The sets τ_CH, τ_CL, and τ_NC partition the task set τ.
T_k is the task whose tardiness is being analyzed.
Jobs in τ_CH have higher priority than T_{k,j} and are pending at t_0.
Jobs in τ_CL have lower priority than T_{k,j} and execute non-preemptively at t_0.
Jobs in τ_NC have priorities such that they do not fall into τ_CH or τ_CL.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides upper bounds on the execution time of jobs from different priority classes (τ_CH, τ_CL, τ_NC) within the critical interval [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ, which is essential for bounding the total demand.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma bounds the amount of work that can be done by tasks in different priority groups within the critical time interval. It leverages the definitions of these groups and the properties of the interval to establish these bounds.
steps: For i = k: The work performed by T_k in [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ cannot exceed the total length of this interval, which is δ_k + (t_e - t_0) + length(Γ). The length of Γ is at most t_d + Θ_k - e_k + 1. The total length of [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ is δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1. Thus, I(T_k) <= δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1.

For i != k: If T_i is in τ_CL, a job T_{i,g} with r_{i,g} < t_0 and T_{i,g} ≻ T_{k,j} executes non-preemptively at t_0. This job can execute for at most e_i - 1 time units if it was already executing before t_0. The total work I_CL(T_i) is bounded by e_i - 1.
The proof for i != k also considers the maximum possible execution time within the interval [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ, which is bounded by the length of the interval itself, max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k).
The bounds are refined based on whether T_i belongs to τ_CH, τ_CL, or τ_NC, considering their priority and execution characteristics within the critical interval.
key_insights: The bounds are derived by considering the maximum possible execution time within the critical interval and the specific execution constraints of tasks in different priority groups.
The definition of Γ (intervals where T_{k,j} does not execute) is crucial for bounding the work done by T_k.

formal_description.statement: I_CL(T_i) is at most min(e_i - 1, δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1), if i = k and D_i >= δ_k + 2 or i > k and D_i >= δ_k + 1, and 0, otherwise.

variables.I_CL(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_CL within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task T_i.
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.

assumptions: T_i is in τ_CL.
A job T_{i,g} with r_{i,g} < t_0 and T_{i,g} ≻ T_{k,j} executes non-preemptively at t_0.
The conditions on D_i are met.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a refined upper bound for the work done by tasks in τ_CL, considering specific conditions on their deadlines relative to the critical interval length.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma refines the bound on work done by tasks in τ_CL by considering specific conditions on their deadlines. If a task's deadline is sufficiently far from the critical interval, its contribution to I_CL might be limited.
steps: If T_i is in τ_CL, a lower-priority job T_{i,g} executes non-preemptively at t_0. This job can execute for at most e_i - 1 time units if it was already executing before t_0.
The total work I_CL(T_i) is bounded by e_i - 1.
Additionally, the work done by T_i cannot exceed the total length of the interval [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ, which is δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1.

The lemma introduces conditions based on D_i relative to δ_k. If D_i is large enough (e.g., D_i >= δ_k + 2 for i=k, or D_i >= δ_k + 1 for i>k), it implies that the job T_{i,g} might not have arrived or its deadline is far beyond the critical interval, thus limiting its execution within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ to 0.
The bound is the minimum of these constraints.
key_insights: The deadline of a task in τ_CL relative to the critical interval length is a key factor in determining its maximum contribution to the demand.
The bound is a combination of the maximum execution time of a single job and the total length of the critical interval.

formal_description.statement: I_NC(T_i) is at most min(DBF(T_i, δ_k), δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1), if i = k, and min(DBF(T_i, δ_k) - e_k, max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k)), if i != k and δ_k >= D_k, and 0, otherwise.

variables.I_NC(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_NC within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.DBF(T_i, δ_k): Demand Bound Function of T_i over an interval of length δ_k, defined as max(0, (δ_k - D_i) / p_i + 1) * e_i.
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.
variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task T_i.

assumptions: T_i is in τ_NC.
Jobs in τ_NC have priorities such that they do not fall into τ_CH or τ_CL.
The conditions on δ_k and D_k are met.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound for the work done by tasks in τ_NC, utilizing the Demand Bound Function (DBF) and considering the critical interval and task parameters.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma bounds the work done by tasks in τ_NC. For tasks not in τ_CH or τ_CL, their demand within the critical interval is bounded by their Demand Bound Function (DBF) over that interval, with adjustments for the specific case of task T_k and when δ_k is large.
steps: Consider T_i in τ_NC. Jobs of T_i executing within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ have release times r_{i,g} >= t_0 and deadlines d_{i,g} <= t_d.
The demand due to such jobs is bounded by the Demand Bound Function (DBF) of T_i over the interval length δ_k.
DBF(T_i, δ_k) = max(0, (δ_k - D_i) / p_i + 1) * e_i.
For i = k: The bound is min(DBF(T_k, δ_k), δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1). The first term is the DBF over the interval, and the second is the total length of the interval.

For i != k and δ_k >= D_k: The bound is min(DBF(T_i, δ_k) - e_i, max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k)). The DBF is adjusted by -e_i because T_{k,j} is not in τ_NC. The second term is the maximum length of the interval where T_i could execute.
If δ_k < D_k, the DBF is 0, leading to a bound of 0.
key_insights: The Demand Bound Function (DBF) is a key tool for bounding the execution demand of tasks over an interval.
The bounds are adjusted based on whether the task is the critical task T_k or a different task, and on the relationship between δ_k and D_k.

formal_description.statement: I_CH(T_i) is at most min(DBF'(T_i, δ_k), δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1), if i = k, and min(DBF'(T_i, δ_k) - e_k, max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k)), if i != k.

variables.I_CH(T_i): Work performed by task T_i in τ_CH within [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ.
variables.DBF'(T_i, δ_k): A modified DBF accounting for jobs released before t_0 and pending at t_0. Defined as δ_k + Θ_i * (e_i / p_i) + min(e_i, (δ_k + Θ_i) mod p_i).
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.
variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task T_i.
variables.Θ_i: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_i.

assumptions: T_i is in τ_CH.
Jobs in τ_CH have higher priority than T_{k,j} and are pending at t_0.
The conditions on δ_k and D_k are met.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound for the work done by tasks in τ_CH, using a modified Demand Bound Function (DBF') that accounts for higher-priority jobs pending at t_0.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma bounds the work done by tasks in τ_CH. These tasks have higher priority and are pending at t_0. The bound uses a modified DBF that accounts for this pre-existing demand.
steps: Consider T_i in τ_CH. These are higher-priority tasks pending at t_0.
The demand of jobs of T_i (excluding T_{k,j} if i=k) released and with deadlines within [t_0, t_d] is bounded by DBF'(T_i, δ_k).
DBF'(T_i, δ_k) = δ_k + Θ_i * (e_i / p_i) + min(e_i, (δ_k + Θ_i) mod p_i). This function accounts for the execution time of jobs released before t_0 and pending at t_0.
For i = k: The bound is min(DBF'(T_k, δ_k), δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1).
For i != k: The bound is min(DBF'(T_i, δ_k) - e_i, max(δ_k - D_k, δ_k - p_k + Θ_k)). The DBF' is adjusted by -e_i, and the second term is the maximum length of the interval.
The proof relies on the fact that jobs in τ_CH are pending at t_0 and have higher priority.
key_insights: The modified DBF' is crucial for accurately bounding the demand of higher-priority tasks that are already active.
The bounds are similar to Lemma 5 but use DBF' to account for the specific characteristics of tasks in τ_CH.

formal_description.statement: If M*(T_k) < m * (δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1) holds for each sporadic task T_k ∈ τ and δ_k ≥ max(min(D_i), min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k)), then no tardiness threshold in τ is violated under NP-GEDF.

variables.M*(T_k): The maximum possible total demand from all tasks in τ within the interval [t_0, t_e) ∪ Γ, considering the optimal assignment of tasks to τ_CH, τ_CL, and τ_NC.
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.

assumptions: The system is scheduled using NP-GEDF.
The condition M*(T_k) < m * (δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1) is checked for all tasks T_k and relevant δ_k values.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a sufficient condition for NP-GEDF schedulability, ensuring that no task exceeds its specified tardiness bound.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem provides the core schedulability test. It states that if the maximum possible demand from all tasks within a critical interval (bounded by M*) is less than the total available processing time on all processors within that interval, then the system is schedulable. The critical interval is defined by the potential tardiness violation of a task T_k.
steps: The theorem is based on the inequality derived from the analysis of the critical job T_{k,j} missing its deadline: Σ_{i=1 to n} I(T_i) ≥ m * (t_d - t_0 + Θ_k - e_k + 1).
This inequality represents the total demand from all tasks versus the total processing capacity.

The paper then defines M(T_k) as the maximum possible value of the LHS (total demand) over all valid assignments of tasks to τ_CH, τ_CL, and τ_NC. M*(T_k) is the maximum of M(T_k) over all possible choices of these sets.
The condition for schedulability is the negation of the demand exceeding capacity: M*(T_k) < m * (δ_k + Θ_k - e_k + 1).
This inequality must hold for every task T_k and for all relevant values of δ_k, which are bounded by Lemma 1 and Theorem 2.
If this condition holds for all tasks T_k and all relevant δ_k, then no task will miss its deadline by more than its allowed tardiness bound.
key_insights: The test is sufficient, not necessary.
It unifies hard and soft real-time analysis by allowing non-zero tardiness bounds (Θ_k).
The complexity arises from determining M*(T_k), which involves finding the optimal assignment of tasks to priority groups.
The condition is checked for a range of δ_k values, which are bounded by Theorem 2.

formal_description.statement: If (10) holds for task T_k for all δ_k ∈ [max(min(D_i), min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k)), δ_max], then (10) holds for all δ_k ≥ max(min(D_i), min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k)).

variables.δ_max: An upper bound on the relevant values of δ_k, defined as (E(m) + U(m-1) * max(Θ_i) + R + m * (e_k - Θ_k - 1)) / (m - U_sum).
variables.E(y): Sum of y largest task execution times.
variables.U(y): Sum of y largest task utilizations.
variables.U_sum: Total utilization of the task system.
variables.e_k: worst-case execution time of task T_k.
variables.Θ_k: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_k.
variables.Θ_i: maximum allowed deadline tardiness for task T_i.

assumptions: The condition in Theorem 1 (Equation 10) is checked.
The task system parameters are within certain bounds (e.g., U_sum < m).
formal_description.conclusion: Bounds the range of δ_k values that need to be checked for the schedulability test, making the test computationally feasible.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is crucial for making the schedulability test practical. It proves that we don't need to check the condition for an infinite number of δ_k values. Instead, we only need to check it up to a certain maximum value (δ_max), because the behavior of the demand function becomes predictable beyond that point.
steps: The schedulability condition in Theorem 1 involves checking an inequality for all δ_k ≥ max(min(D_i), min(D_k, p_k - Θ_k)).
This would be computationally intractable if we had to check infinitely many values.
Theorem 2 establishes an upper bound, δ_max, for the range of δ_k that needs to be checked.
The proof relies on the fact that the Demand Bound Function (DBF) and the calculation of M*(T_k) change values only at specific points (when DBF(T_i, δ_k) changes for some T_i).
The upper bound δ_max is derived by considering the maximum possible values of task parameters and system utilization.
If the condition holds for all δ_k within the interval [lower_bound, δ_max], it is guaranteed to hold for all δ_k beyond δ_max.
key_insights: Reduces the infinite search space for δ_k to a finite one.
The definition of δ_max is complex, involving sums of execution times, utilizations, and tardiness bounds.
This theorem is what enables the pseudo-polynomial time complexity of the schedulability test.
